fatal_errors: The hypothesis attributes resistance to the intrinsic chromium passivity of a generic high-Cr steel rather than reconstructing the atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L.
It omits the governing 550 °C for 2 h post-coating anneal, the associated grain refinement and BCC/FCC microstructure, and the comparison with as-sprayed and uncoated SS316L.
Its proposed ambient-to-300 °C chloride or high-temperature-water exposures do not match the demonstrated 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or 900 °C cyclic molten-salt exposures.
The irradiation-dependent self-repair mechanism is speculative and unsupported by cited evidence.
explanation: The response is scientifically plausible as a general stainless-steel passivation hypothesis and proposes useful TEM/XPS, polarization, and EIS measurements with composition and grain-size controls. It also gives reasonable qualitative boundaries and an explicit falsification rule. However, it largely misses the target material system and intervention: an approximately 150 µm AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating deposited by atmospheric plasma spraying on SS316L and annealed at several temperatures, with 550 °C for 2 h identified as optimal. The only substantive mechanistic overlap is formation of a protective Cr-rich oxide and resulting lower corrosion current or improved passivity. It omits Al-rich oxides, sluggish-diffusion effects, BCC-dominated coating structure, pore and crack penetration by chloride/sulphide/vanadate species, hot-corrosion mass gain, and the loss of hardness above 550 °C. Its baselines are internally sensible but do not reproduce the relevant uncoated, as-sprayed, and annealed controls. No prior findings are actually cited, so the claimed support—especially for irradiation-enhanced film repair—has weak evidence discipline.
